title: Loss, Rescue, and Equal Shares
overview: David returns to find his town burned and every family taken, then recovers them all and insists that everyone in his band shares the plunder equally.

parts.label: Coming home to ashes (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Sent home from the Philistine army, David's men find Ziklag burned and their families carried off alive, likely to be kept or sold as slaves, perhaps in revenge for David's own deadly raids on the Amalekites earlier. Bitter with grief over their sons and daughters, the men talk of stoning David, but he finds strength in God.

parts.label: Asking God, starting the chase (vv. 7-10)
parts.note: The ephod was a priestly garment used to seek God's answer, probably by casting sacred lots, and David asks before acting. At the Besor ravine, a seasonal stream south of Gaza, a third of his men are too worn out to go on and stay behind.

parts.label: A slave left to die (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: An Egyptian slave, abandoned by his Amalekite master when he fell sick, is found starving, and David's men feed him until he revives. In return for a solemn promise of safety, he leads them to the raiders, so the man left behind becomes the key to the rescue.

parts.label: The raid and the rescue (vv. 16-20)
parts.note: The Amalekites, thinking David is far away, are celebrating their loot when he attacks and fights them from dusk to the next evening, killing all but four hundred who escape on camels. The text is plain about the slaughter, and it stresses that every captive is brought back and nothing is missing, along with much extra plunder.

parts.label: Everyone shares alike (vv. 21-25)
parts.note: Some of the fighters want to give the men who stayed behind nothing but their families back. David refuses, calling the victory a gift from God rather than their own achievement, and equal shares for those who guard supplies became a lasting rule in Israel.

parts.label: Gifts to Judah's towns (vv. 26-31)
parts.note: David sends some of the plunder to leaders in towns of his own tribe, Judah, places where he and his men had moved about while on the run. It reads as gratitude, and many readers also see a shrewd move to build support just before Saul's death opens the way for David to become king.

think: When everything falls apart at once, what do you reach for to steady yourself?
